name: Don Quixote
info: Don Quixote is a Spanish novel by Miguel de Cervantes, published in two parts in 1605 and 1615, about a gentleman of La Mancha who reads so many chivalric romances that he sets out as a knight-errant; it is regarded as the first modern novel.

facts.made: Miguel de Cervantes, who sold the rights to Part One to the publisher-bookseller Francisco de Robles in July 1604; Part Two followed in 1615, a year before his death
facts.form: A prose novel in Early Modern Spanish, published in two parts in 1605 and 1615, episodic in structure, with several interpolated stories told by minor characters
facts.where: Read in printed editions and translations; the Cervantes Collection at the State Library of New South Wales holds over 1,100 editions, and the Library of Congress and the Biblioteca de Catalunya hold collections of early volumes
facts.known: Don Quixote and Sancho Panza; the attack on the windmills; Rocinante and Dulcinea del Toboso; the Part Two characters who have read Part One; the word quixotic; the spurious sequel by Avellaneda; one of the most-translated books in the world

t: A hidalgo of La Mancha who reads too many chivalric romances sets out as the knight-errant Don Quixote, with the farm labourer Sancho Panza as his squire, and Cervantes spoofs the romances through the retelling of his acts.

Published in 1605, the book was an immediate success and was translated into French, German, Italian and English within seven years of its appearance; a spurious sequel in 1614 pushed Cervantes to publish his own Part Two in 1615.
Part Two is an early example of metafiction, with characters who have read Part One, and the novel has given English the adjective quixotic and the phrase tilting at windmills.
dyk: In 2002 the Norwegian Nobel Institute asked writers from 55 countries to choose the greatest work of fiction ever written, and the majority voted for Don Quixote.
ev: Cervantes sells the rights to Don Quixote, Part One, to the publisher-bookseller Francisco de Robles for an unknown sum
Part One appears in Madrid, and by August there are two Madrid editions, two Lisbon editions and one in Valencia
Thomas Shelton's English translation of Part One appears while Cervantes is still alive
A spurious second part by an author using the name Avellaneda is published in Tarragona
Cervantes publishes his own Part Two, finished as a direct result of the Avellaneda book
Parts One and Two are published together as one edition in Barcelona
John Ormsby's translation appears and becomes the model for most modern English translators

sections.origins:
Cervantes wrote at a time when, as the novel is said to reflect, Spain's standing as a world power was declining and its national treasury was bankrupt because of expensive foreign wars. The Protestant Reformation had put the Spanish Roman Catholic Church on the defensive, which had led to the establishment of the Spanish Inquisition, and the hidalgo class was losing relevance as changes in society made the high ideals of chivalry obsolete.

The book draws on earlier literature. Its sources include the Castilian novel Amadis de Gaula, which had been very popular throughout the 16th century, and Tirant lo Blanch, which the priest in the novel calls the best book in the world, though in what sense it was best is much debated among scholars. Cervantes also refers to the Italian poem Orlando furioso, and Apuleius's The Golden Ass appears to have been another important source. His experiences as a galley slave in Algiers also influenced the work, as did his family's ties to the medical community. Tradition in Argamasilla de Alba holds that he was imprisoned in the cave of Medrano and began the book there.
sections.content:
Alonso Quixano is an hidalgo nearing 50 who lives in an unspecified region of La Mancha with his niece and housekeeper. His obsession with chivalric romances leads him to don an old suit of armour, rename himself Don Quixote, name his workhorse Rocinante and make Aldonza Lorenzo, whom he renames Dulcinea del Toboso, his lady. He takes an inn for a castle and is dubbed a knight by the innkeeper in a pretend ceremony. He then recruits his neighbour, the poor farm labourer Sancho Panza, as squire, with the promise of a petty governorship, and attacks windmills that he takes for giants.

In Part One he imposes his imagination on the world, while Sancho's spirit ascends from reality to illusion, as Salvador de Madariaga put it. The book also contains tales told by other characters, the best known being The Ill-Advised Curiosity, about a Florentine nobleman who has a friend try to seduce his wife. In Part Two a duke and duchess who have read Part One stage practical jokes on the pair, Sancho gets a false governorship, and Don Quixote is defeated by the Knight of the White Moon and ordered to give up chivalry for a year. He then falls ill, regains his sanity as Alonso Quixano, renounces his ambition and dies.
sections.making:
For Cervantes and the readers of his day, Don Quixote was a one-volume book published in 1605, divided internally into four parts. The mention of further adventures at its close was conventional and was not taken seriously as a plan for a continuation. In July 1604 Cervantes sold the rights to the publisher-bookseller Francisco de Robles; the licence to publish was granted in September, the printing was finished in December, and the book came out on 16 January 1605. The sale deprived him of further profit on Part One.

In about September 1614 a spurious Part Two appeared in Tarragona under the name of Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda, by an unidentified Aragonese who admired Lope de Vega. Its prologue insulted Cervantes, who took offence. He had probably not got much further than Chapter 59 by late July 1614. His own Part Two, published in 1615, takes up the matter: Don Quixote finds Avellaneda's book being printed in Barcelona and meets one of its characters, Don Alvaro Tarfe, whom he makes swear that the other Quixote and Sancho are impostors. Avellaneda's identity has been the subject of many theories, with no consensus.
sections.reception:
The novel was an immediate success. By August 1605 there were two Madrid editions, two published in Lisbon and one in Valencia, and pirated editions were soon being prepared. Most of the 400 copies of the first edition were sent to the New World, and although most disappeared in a shipwreck near Havana, about 70 reached Lima and were sent on to Cuzco. Seven years after Part One appeared, it had been translated into French, German, Italian and English.

Readers have taken the book in different ways. Harold Bloom calls it the first modern novel and says its recurring theme is the human need to withstand suffering. Edith Grossman describes first reading it as the most tragic book in the world and later laughing aloud while translating it, since Cervantes never lets the reader rest. Some critics regard Part Two as better than Part One for its depth of characterisation and its philosophical insights. The book has also been said to have smiled Spain's chivalry away. Mark Twain said it swept the world's admiration for mediaeval chivalry out of existence. In 1632 Cardinal Zapata ordered one sentence, on works of charity done in a lukewarm way, removed from future editions.
sections.survival:
The book has survived through printing, and its history is one of editions. After the early printings in Madrid, Lisbon, Valencia and Brussels, a third Madrid edition appeared in 1608, a seventh publication in all, and a Milan bookseller issued an Italian edition in 1610. Parts One and Two were first published as one edition in Barcelona in 1617. The novel is believed to have sold more than 500 million copies worldwide, and the Cervantes Collection at the State Library of New South Wales, gathered by Ben Haneman over thirty years, includes over 1,100 editions.

English translation has its own history. Thomas Shelton's version of Part One appeared in 1612 and of Part Two in 1620, though John Ormsby and Samuel Putnam found it far from satisfactory. Pierre Antoine Motteux's version of around 1700 was reprinted until recent times, yet Ormsby called it worse than worthless. The Jervas translation of 1742, printed as Jarvis through an error, was the most frequently reprinted until about 1885, and Tobias Smollett's of 1755 is still reprinted. Most modern translators take John Ormsby's of 1885 as their model, and Daniel Eisenberg, reviewing 27 of 30 English translations in 2008, found no single ideal one.
sections.legacy:
The book had a major influence on the literary community and is directly referenced in 19th-century French works such as Alexandre Dumas's The Three Musketeers and Edmond Rostand's Cyrano de Bergerac. Its pair of characters, the tall, thin, idealistic Quixote and the fat, world-weary Panza, became a motif echoed ever since, and Sancho Panza and Rocinante are emblems of Western literary culture. It has inspired works by Pablo Picasso and Richard Strauss, and the French opera Don Quichotte.

The language took in its terms. The word quixotic, defined by Merriam-Webster as the foolishly impractical pursuit of ideals, was quickly adopted by many languages, and tilting at windmills, meaning attacking imaginary enemies, comes from the scene of the windmills. The phrase the pot calling the kettle black also has its own article. The opening sentence created a classic Spanish cliche with de cuyo nombre no quiero acordarme. Species have been named after the novel and its characters, among them the amphipod Dulcibella camanchaca and the dinosaurs Lohuecotitan pandafilandi and Qunkasaura pintiquiniestra.

summary: Don Quixote is Cervantes's Spanish novel of a gentleman of La Mancha who, after reading too many chivalric romances, sets out as a knight-errant with Sancho Panza. Published in 1605 and 1615, it is regarded as the first modern novel and one of the most-translated books in the world.
notes: The article gives no manuscripts or surviving copies of Cervantes's text, so 'where' and 'survival' speak of printed editions and the collections the article names.
The article says the 1605 first edition was 400 copies, most sent to the New World; 'unknown sum' for the rights is the article's.
The article calls the book both 'the first modern novel' and 'the greatest work ever written' (some); the latter is reported only through the 2002 Nobel Institute poll.
The article says Avellaneda's book was published 'in about September' 1614 in one place and 'in 1614' in another; the same year in both.
The article says Cervantes died 'a year' after Part Two (1615), so 1616 is not stated as a figure beyond 'a year before his own death'.

Left out: the article's long lists of English translations beyond those named, the pronunciation history of Quixote, the Villanueva de los Infantes location theory, the interpolated-story plot detail beyond one sentence.
